speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many do not realise how important a role our land transport and public transportation plays.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And if I may add, what are the spending needs that will be required for this Budget and for the next few Budgets down the road?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we add more stations to cater for the newly-developed sites, will we also be rationalising our train system and probably shut down certain stations possibly where footfall may have permanently plunged?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does our 2030 target also envisage the removal or subtraction of train stations?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Ministry share the current and future enhancements to our last-mile transport connectivity to homes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, the use of autonomous vehicles in the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially important as our society ages rapidly and many of our residents become possibly less mobile down the road.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Public transport cost is not immuned, with the recent public transport fare hike of $0.10 to $0.11 per journey.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In addition, the Government also has made available public transport vouchers to help low-income households cover about six months of the fare increase.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can the Ministry share an update on efforts to ensure our public transport system will remain affordable for Singaporeans over the next decade and more?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What other transport welfare schemes could potentially be rolled out to help vulnerable Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Subject to budget constraints, can we consider introducing transport vouchers as part of the regular Budget cycle, akin to the Community Development Council (CDC) Vouchers, to help mitigate the impact of rising costs for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I do note that our bus and rail services were already operating at a loss before the pandemic struck and ridership has yet to recover to pre-pandemic levels.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What would additional transport welfare entail from a financial sustainability perspective?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With the extensive upgrading of our rail infrastructure then, continuous upskilling was needed to ensure that workers kept up with new technologies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We will also see the completion of the Singapore-Johor Bahru Rapid Transit System in 2026.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Given that the COVID-19 pandemic had stymied training for about two years, I would like to ask how much funds remain in the RMDP, which is set to expire this year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that MOT can extend, and perhaps even top up the RMDP, so that we can continue growing our skilled workforce to support the expanding and increasingly complex rail network.

speaker: The Chairman
text: You have two cuts, please take them together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Cross Island Line (CRL) will be our longest fully underground MRT line, serving the eastern, western and north-eastern corridors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When operational, its seven interchange stations will provide even more alternative travel routes for commuters.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Phase 1 of the CRL is targeted to be completed by 2030.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The target date for the completion of Phase 2 is yet to be finalised.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The CRL – Punggol Extension is expected to be completed by 2032, serving commuters travelling to Pasir Ris, Tampines North, Punggol and Sengkang.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider lengthening the Extension to connect to Fernvale, Yio Chu Kang and Lentor stations for resilience purposes?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will provide more alternatives for commuters to switch to the TEL and NEL to travel to the west and north in the event of breakdowns and other circumstances.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At last year’s Committee of Supply (COS), I requested MOT to consider providing more city direct bus services during the morning peak hours.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am grateful that the Land Transport Authority (LTA) acceded to my appeal and had since provided an additional trip by SBS Transit City Direct Bus Service 671 to serve commuters from Sengkang to the Central Business District.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As noted by the Ministry, the ridership has been increasing as more residents move into the new Build-To-Order (BTO) flats at Fernvale.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Residents still find that the additional trip is not quite sufficient.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, may I ask if MOT could consider working with private bus operators to provide additional trips during the morning peak hour?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I recently asked ChatGPT what it thought of the Singapore public transport system.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Its reply: “Singapore’s public transport system is widely regarded as one of the best in the world”.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Descriptors ChatGPT used include “efficiency”, “extensive coverage”, “integration”, “accessibility”, “cleanliness and safety” and “affordability”.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On accessibility, ChatGPT says: “Singapore’s public transportation system is designed to be accessible to people with disabilities and the elderly.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, an inclusive public transport system goes beyond hardware.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to a May 2022 CNA article, the wheelchair ramp on buses has become a source of anxiety, especially amongst new wheelchair users.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the same article, Mikail Wong who became a wheelchair user not long before the article was published shared: “When I’m going to take the bus, other commuters might look at me.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Am I hindering others?” While we have definitely provided hardware that is more inclusive, how else can we grow a more caring commuter culture so that persons with disabilities, seniors and families with young children can use our public transportation system and amenities with just as much ease as the rest of us?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Chair, MOT must ensure that prominent and informative captions or visuals accompany audio announcements, during times of service disruption.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Could MOT also explore complementary forms of communication, such as text message alerts or mobile applications, to reach commuters who may not be able to hear announcements over the loudspeaker?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This will work better than passive communication channels where the commuter has to search online or approach staff to find out more information.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I seek an update from the Ministry regarding the review of the point-to-point (P2P) transport industry.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, the environment has evolved for our P2P drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The introduction of ride-hail services and the use of apps for booking transport have changed commuter behaviours and preferences.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The escalating costs of business which includes petrol prices, rental fees and maintenance costs have put immense pressure on our P2P drivers, many who have taken to driving upwards of 14 hours in a day to make ends meet.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our drivers are also reeling from the two years of almost no income and are catching up on rebuilding their nest eggs after dipping into their retirement savings to get by during COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we look to rationalising and revitalising our P2P business models – between ride-hail/street-hail, taxi/platforms – it is important to note that our drivers have also indicated their growing insecurities with their earnings, welfare and benefits with their platform partners.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The lack of transparency when it comes to distribution of work, price fluctuations and campaigns do impact the earnings of our drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some of our drivers say that they find themselves struggling to make ends meet due to hidden costs and unclear earnings structures.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, unlike the true self-employed, our platform drivers are subject to management controls.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the review, can the Ministry consider putting in more safeguards to protect the earnings of our drivers, especially if we see a convergence of more drivers offering ride-hail services.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: It would carefully study the pros and cons first.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, with the 2014 announcement of Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) 2.0 and the progressive roll-out of the new vehicle On-Board Units (OBUs) from November 2023, an alternative solution has emerged.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is argued that emissions, congestion and accidents are externalities of car usage, which can be tackled by distance-based charging instead of limiting car ownership.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: LTA has stated that there are “no immediate plans to introduce distance-based charging”, even though the new system is capable of doing so.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: While distance-based charging could make ERP fairer by charging motorists for their road usage, rather than whether they go past a certain point, challenges include the reliability and accuracy of satellite-based tracking in Singapore’s dense urban environment and wider policy implications on high-mileage industries like logistics and transportation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Our car-lite vision does not mean a car-free society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Would the Minister help explain whether they would introduce a distance-based charging, which allows us to increase the vehicle population, while achieving our car-lite vision?

speaker: The Chairman
text: You have two cuts, please take them together.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, vehicle ownership may not correlate directly to road traffic conditions, nor compared to actual vehicle usage.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister share if there are improvements in the present overall roadway traffic density and peak-hour conditions compared to pre-pandemic period?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister also share the trends in the transportation modal split over the past six years since the implementation of zero-growth policy?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Has there been a decline in private vehicle usage, especially so as the PHCs have become prevalent in recent years?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There are some challenges getting vehicle owners to switch to electric vehicles (EVs).

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Lastly, a robust second-hand market is still absent, posing difficulties for financiers and operators to assess the risk of investing in commercial EVs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How do the statistics compare to those for commercial vehicle sales?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Will MOT introduce more incentives to encourage take-up of EVs for commercial use?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: A crucial objective of EV conversion is to mitigate carbon emissions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Therefore, it is imperative to prioritise the conversion of vehicles used for higher mileage.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: One prominent group of such users comprises taxi and PHC drivers, who typically cover a range of 200 to 300 kilometres per day during a single shift.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If you are on double shift, it could be up to 450 kilometres.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Given their extensive coverage, relying solely on overnight charging via slow chargers at the HDB car parks may not suffice to sustain their daily operations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Additional fast charging sessions during breaks, such as lunch or dinner, become necessary.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I propose that LTA strategically installs fast chargers near high-traffic hawker centres and major eateries to enhance operational efficiency for these drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Such a initiative would incentivise more taxi and PHC drivers to transition to EVs, thereby benefiting not only themselves but also contributing to the well-being of the planet.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The roll-out of EVs in Singapore has the potential to significantly impact P2P drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Our drivers rely on efficient and accessible charging stations to maintain their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: We seek clarification from the Ministry on the measures in place to ensure that P2P drivers have adequate access to EV charging stations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Has the Ministry conducted studies on high flow P2P locations and rest locations which are convenient and not out of place for our drivers?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Together with locations where there are no parking fees, will these locations be prioritised in the roll-out?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Furthermore, the transition to EVs will require P2P drivers to bear additional costs, such as the upgrading of their current vehicles and purchasing or leasing EVs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Some PHC drivers may also experience penalties for the early terminations of their current rental contracts with rental companies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Will the Ministry consider providing financial support for our drivers during this transition?

speaker: The Chairman
text: You have two cuts, please take them together.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I asked that we look into having faster EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I am glad that within my constituency and many other parts of Singapore, there are more and more EV points being installed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Indeed, this is good a good sign as many car owners are conscious of the need to be green and sustainable, and hence, more residents are buying EVs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What if an EV owner parks his car at a charging point for several days because he is away on holiday?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He will be depriving other EVs owners use of the EV charging point.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And this would be essential, especially for high mileage drivers like taxi drivers or PHC drivers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I receive frequent complaints from residents that cars drive at high speed in residential areas, where there may be seniors or young children using the roads.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also received complaints about vehicles that do not slow down at zebra crossings, even though the zebra crossings are raised crossing.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have also seen motorcycles cutting across pedestrian footpaths, just to save on parking charges.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: After all, road safety should be the concern of all road users and not just motorists.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Pedestrians who walk onto the zebra crossing without keeping a look out for cars, or pedestrians who watch videos or are obsessed with their mobile devices are taking unnecessary risks with their lives and this should not be the case.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, one life lost is one too many.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should not take road safety for granted.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Traffic accidents are avoidable if everyone plays his or her part.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The latest statistics published by the Traffic Police are sobering.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a society, it is time for us to review how we can improve safety on our roads, be it for pedestrians, cyclists or motorists.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government has imposed stiffer penalties, stepped up enforcement and implemented traffic calming measures, to try to modify the behaviour of drivers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Indeed, with the Traffic Police's announcement that they will be enlisting the help of their network of red-light cameras to catch speeding cases as well, I am hopeful that it can act as an effective deterrent against motorists who decide to speed when it appears that no one is watching.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am also reassured by recent comments by LTA and the Traffic Police that ground assessments, and enforcement actions, are constantly and frequently conducted at accident and violation-prone hot spots.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to put all errant motorists on guard as soon as we can.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perhaps then, everyone should drive or ride as though there are speed cameras everywhere, if this is what it takes to prevent yet another senseless loss of life or limb.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have deterrent measures, but we also need to implement measures that can modify the behaviour of motorists.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I would like to call upon the MOT to consider investing more resources into prioritising the roll-out of additional traffic-calming measures, in high-risk or accident-prone areas.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even if the accidents did not lead to fatalities, a higher-than-usual accident rate may mean that it is probably a matter of time before something really bad happens.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With a greying population, we should expect that we may start to need more Silver Zones in the future.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is commendable that LTA and Traffic Police also work closely with the wider community, including our schools and the Singapore Road Safety Council, on road safety campaigns.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that LTA can expand its very important Safe Route to School projects to work with more schools, including private schools and preschools, as well as locations with a high density of enrichment or after-school care centres, to map out students' walking patterns and identify safe-walking routes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These modifications include non-compliant exhaust and lighting systems, as well as tinted windows.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For illegal modifications that change the speed of or even compromise the handling of the vehicle, I hope that LTA can deploy more resources to catch these offenders.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ask anyone who has been driving regularly on Singapore's roads for the past 20 years and you would likely get unfavourable comments about the behaviours of many of our drivers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This observation is borne out by the Traffic Police statistics showing a significant increase in the number of accidents where the cause was the motorist failing to keep a proper lookout, failing to have proper control of the vehicle or changing of lanes without due care.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ask any driver too, and they will tell you that on a daily basis, they encounter pedestrians crossing the roads without checking for vehicles or are jaywalking and also many who are engrossed in their mobile phones, or even wearing noise-cancelling earphones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Education campaigns, road design, penalties and enforcement are very critical measures in modifying the behaviour of our road users, but perhaps, we need to address the underlying issues, borne out of life in a busy, urban city where people always seem to be in a rush and have less patience on the roads.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How many innocent lives have to be lost before our society realises that everyone – be it pedestrians or motorists, needs to just slow down and pay full attention when on our roads?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The time is high for a fundamental shift in mindset, culture and behaviours.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government cannot do this alone, each and every one of us has an important part to play.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The Friendly Streets pilot, launched just last year, is a welcomed move as it builds gracious neighbourhoods and inclusive communities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: No doubt, in a bustling new town like Punggol, with its park connectors, walkable precincts and penchant for sustainable cycling commutes, Friendly Streets will make our neighbourhoods more convenient, comfortable and safe for our pedestrians and cyclists.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: How will these streets be seamlessly integrated into our existing infrastructure, to ensure a cohesive and sustainable urban environment?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Can Friendly Streets also be expanded to include better support for our delivery riders?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: And finally, in the roll-out plans for other new neighbourhoods, will proactive-mobility towns, like Punggol, be featured in next rollout of Friendly Streets?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Since 2013, and on several occasions in this House thereafter, I have consistently urged LTA to consider expanding the covered walkway network to connect not only to MRT stations and bus interchanges, but also to other significant bus stops.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Given Singapore's hot and humid weather, coupled with occasional rain, as well as its ageing population, I strongly urge LTA to prioritise making the first-mile and last-mile walking journeys more accessible, more comfortable and more convenient at all major bus stops across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Enhancing the walking experience not only helps to improve public transport ridership, it also contributes to promoting a healthy lifestyle, meeting our Healthier SG objective.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Should LTA face financial constraints, I propose that MOT collaborates with the Ministry of Health (MOH) to leverage on the Healthier SG fund for more covered walkways.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Improving the walking experience requires a coordinated effort across various Government departments and agencies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to request that if LTA is to implement this suggestion, please do consider my ward, Kaki Bukit, for its pilot as it is one of the first few estates to have a Silver Zone.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Sadly, Kaki Bukit does not even have a single sheltered linkway erected by LTA at pedestrian crossings, although I have previously sent written requests to LTA for such improvements.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: With the increase in the use of PMAs by the elderly and physically disabled, widening such areas would enhance the safety and comfort for all users.

speaker: Mdm Chairman
text: Ms Poh Li San, you have two cuts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry share details of the plans for the nationwide transformation of our transport framework and design, to enable the elderly to commute more conveniently and safely?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How does the Ministry intend to make use of the Age Well SG funding, to make it easier and more comfortable for seniors to move around in their neighbourhoods, so that they can continue to lead active lifestyles and age gracefully in their communities?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: As there will be more Personal Mobility Aids (PMAs) and wheelchair users with the increasing number of elderly, does MOT intend to widen pedestrian and shared paths, and create parking spaces for PMAs, especially in older neighbourhood estates?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: PMAs have been widely used in recent years, mainly by the elderly and those with mobility issues.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: However, there is a growing trend, including in Sembawang West, where some young people with no visible disabilities or health issues, are also using PMAs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Some of them drive them at high speeds, with little regard for the safety of others in their vicinity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Most of them are using their PMAs to deliver food and other items, so they are probably rushing deliveries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Can seniors above a certain age, for instance, above 65, automatically qualify as eligible users, even without medical certification?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Separately, what can owners who do not meet the medical criteria do with their PMAs if they are not able to use them anymore?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The situation has improved greatly with more enforcement by LTA officers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Many cyclists have also improved their behaviour to become more gracious when they see pedestrians on the shared footpaths.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: However, lately, I have started to receive complaints about the use of PMAs by able-bodied persons who use these PMAs as a means of transport.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: They ride the heavy PMAs into shopping malls and at places where there are also pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: And some ride the PMAs at a faster speed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This represents a hazard or danger to other users of the same space.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Other than regulations, may I urge LTA to do more to promote gracious behaviour among all commuters, including pedestrians, PMA users, cyclists, motorists and PMD users.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: There should be mutual respect for one another and we should not always take the attitude that we have the right of way all the time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I agree that there should be a reasonable speed limit, given the risk of collisions with pedestrians sharing the same path.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Having said that, I also received feedback that a speed of six kilometres per hour is a bit too slow, especially for some seniors who are used to using mobility scooters to travel beyond their immediate neighbourhoods and the reduced speed would also mean longer travelling time for some.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I understand that six kilometres per hour is tied to average walking speed, but I wonder whether the proposed speed can be slightly higher than six kilometres per hour, at least for wider or less busy paths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope this medical certification restriction will not be applied too rigidly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some seniors may not be able to walk very far before they need to rest, due to declining physical ability, and not necessarily due to serious illness or diagnosed conditions with their lower limbs or spinal areas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: PMAs do provide seniors with confidence to be out and about, which is a good thing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Like enforcement against illegal use of PMDs, such as e-scooters or hoverboards on roads or footpaths, which unfortunately we still see today, though less frequently than before, for the new measures to work effectively, there must be regular enforcement against illegal or unsafe use as well as against non-compliant mobility scooters, as the lack of enforcement will encourage non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Regarding enforcement efforts against PMAs able to travel beyond the prescribed speed, I note that for current e-bikes, though there may be officers at certain busy spots carrying out spot checks, we still see e-bikes exceeding the permitted speed limits, sometimes even on par with the vehicles travelling alongside them on the roads, far exceeding the 25 kilometres per hour limit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope LTA will consider more stringent enforcement measures to deter speeding for all mobility devices, including measures against shops that help to tweak the speed mechanisms of devices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Regular enforcement must come hand in hand with good public education.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: LTA must consider how to push out the messaging on the new rules via mainstream and social media to achieve good public knowledge and consciousness.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Public education should not be merely for the mobility scooter users, but for the public at large.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Public knowledge of what is allowed and what is no allowed will, I believe, enhance compliance and encourage considerate use by all.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In our pursuit of safer and more inclusive public paths, we must also recognise the challenges faced by those who rely on PMAs for their primary livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As we consider strengthening regulations on PMAs, it is essential to approach this issue with empathy and understanding for all stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The upcoming regulations aimed at enhancing safety and reducing misuse have raised concerns amongst our PWD food delivery and courier riders.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Reducing speed limits for PMAs will affect delivery riders in terms of the number of orders accepted, in turn, affecting their livelihood for earnings.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Some of our riders who use PMAs have long-term disabilities or are frail due to age or chronic illnesses.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: However, not all have medical letters or medical certificates to qualify for having a PMA.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Some have medical letters which have expired or lapsed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In such cases, how can these riders be better supported to obtain the clearance for the use of PMAs?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Safety is a priority and gracious use of our walkways and roads are paramount.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Implementation of strengthened regulations, however, must be fair and equitable for all stakeholders and our PWD riders’ interest must continue to be safeguarded.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: One reason is the jump in the number of seemingly able-bodied persons using them for transportation, especially for food deliveries.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Many of them speed along walking paths, posing a danger to all pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The panel also asked for enforcement to be stepped up with penalties.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What has been the progress of the adoption of these recommendations so far to date?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Accidents often occur along footpaths due to a lack of awareness and courtesy among pedestrians, cyclists and PMD users.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some of my residents have suffered severe injuries as a result.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I call on the Ministry to conduct more public safety education for all footpath users.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For instance, cyclists should be encouraged to sound their bell when they are some distance away from pedestrians to alert them of their approach and not wait until they are directly behind.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Pedestrians should be educated to avoid suddenly changing direction without looking over their shoulders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Cyclists who disregard pedestrian safety should be taken to task.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By promoting a culture of mutual respect and responsibility, we can make our footpaths safer and more pleasant for everyone.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is not only a matter of convenience but also of public health and social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: With the recent completion of new cycling paths spanning from East Coast Park to Pasir Ris Park, cyclists, especially those residing in the East, now enjoy added convenience.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: However, there remains a pressing need for more cycling infrastructure in the West, particularly for residents in the far-western areas like Nanyang.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I, therefore, kindly request an update from MOT regarding the cycling path plan for the Western region, specifically in the Nanyang, Gek Poh and Pioneer estates, whether they have the progress of these plans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: One resident from Nanyang expressed his aspiration for a cycling path connecting his HDB void deck to Pioneer or Boon Lay MRT station, as well as to Jurong Lake Garden which was just completed last year, thereby providing seamless connectivity to the rest of the island through Park Connectors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I earnestly hope that MOT can work towards realising his dream earlier rather than later.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on whether any discussions have been held with our Malaysian counterparts and what is the progress of the project to date?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In view of the resurgence of shipping activities post-COVID-19 and with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) declaring a record annual vessel arrival tonnage at the Port of Singapore last year, I would like to seek an update from MOT regarding the readiness of our ports to accommodate the rising demand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Specifically, I am keen to know if the Mega Port Development in Tuas is on schedule.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In addition, I would also like to ask what is the current workforce size at the Tuas port as of February 2024?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Are there any strategies in place to enhance connectivity for the benefit of port workers?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Meanwhile, I understand that many PSA port workers rely on chartered bus services provided at PSA for transportation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: However, I am concerned about the sustainability of this arrangement in the long run.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Therefore, I enquire if there are plans to introduce a feeder bus service connecting Tuas port with the nearest MRT station, which is Tuas Link MRT station, to address this concern.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: As we continue to develop the Tuas port, it is essential to prioritise the welfare of our port workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I look forward to receiving updates on these matters from MOT.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: What are MOT’s plans to ensure a strong pipeline of skilled workforce to support the industry’s continued growth?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: How does MOT plan to lower the training barriers so that our existing maritime workforce can upskill and reskill to meet the changing needs of the sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can MOT provide an update on the development of the Tuas Mega Port?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Understandably, there have been some teething transport issues, particularly in terms of public transport accessibility.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: In response, a working committee was set up last year to look into the transportation challenges.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can MOT provide an update on the plans to improve public transport accessibility at Tuas Port?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can we expedite the construction of the viaduct leading to Tuas South before container traffic is expected to surge due to the operational start date of the Port Plus Hub some time in 2027, 2028?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: How does MOT plan to make the area around Tuas Port a better place to work so that workers will be attracted to join our maritime companies based there and help our maritime sector continue its growth story?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What is Singapore doing to catalyse the adoption of green maritime solutions?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The Energy Observer, the world’s first hydrogen-powered ship, docked in Singapore for a 10-day stopover in March 2022.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Are there plans for subsequent phases of Tuas Port development to cater to maritime vessels using hydrogen fuel in the future?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Also, how will the Government ensure the safety and supply of alternative marine fuels?

speaker: The Chairman
text: You have two cuts, you can take them together.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The ports will also be adopting electrified equipment and vehicles, energy-saving infrastructure and solar energy generation to offset electricity consumption.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We are enhancing port efficiency, which can improve the sustainability of the maritime sector on top of cost savings for businesses.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Even the international shipping industry has responded by exploring the use of alternative fuels, such as hydrogen, methanol and ammonia.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This is shown by the growing order books for methanol and ammonia fuelled new-builds and retrofits.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, what measures are being taken to develop safety standards and operational procedures and prepare the workforce to handle these new fuels safely?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Recent events, such as the Russia-Ukraine conflict and United States-China geopolitical tensions have led to a reconfiguration of global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, the past few years have seen disruptions in the global supply networks with port shutdowns during the pandemic and the Houthi Attacks in the Red Sea and the droughts at the Panama Canal.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also emerging trends towards renewable energy and the economic growth of regions in Asia Pacific and in Latin America could lead to further adjustments in supply chain dynamics.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In response, many companies are shifting from efficiency towards resilience and moving away from "just in time" to "just in case", by diversifying their supply chains.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, some of the strategies businesses are employing include shifting or commencing manufacturing in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Our neighbours, Malaysia and Indonesia, are also attracting foreign investment for manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While companies have also increasingly expanded their supply chain functions in Singapore, we are also seeing heightened competition from neighbours.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: With the robust connectivity and increased capacity at the port and airport in the future, Singapore is well-positioned to take advantage of the opportunities arising from these shifts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Hundreds of container ships are re-routing from the Red Sea to go around the Cape of Good Hope at Africa's southern tip, adding around 10 to 15 days to their voyages.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Presumably, that is not only due to our central location on these important trade routes, but also the safe and efficient operations of our port.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Yet, other indicators are also relevant if we are to serve as a "catch-up" port for ships that face delays in other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: A Statista report published in November 2023 showed that shipping vessels spent a median time of about 0.76 days in the Port of Singapore in 2022, a longer time spent within the port's vicinity compared to the previous years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How can Singapore enhance our port services to maintain the competitiveness of our port and continue facilitating the smooth functioning of supply chains amidst recent disruptions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The transport sector provides a wide array of jobs, from operating our aviation and maritime hubs, to powering 6.4 million daily public transport journeys, to supporting those activities up the supply chain like maintenance and repair.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The move of port operations to the new Tuas Mega Port will also require manpower.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Concurrently, our ageing population and reduction in foreign worker dependency could add to the supply crunch in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is before we even consider the growth areas of green transportation and digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can the Ministry share what types of jobs in the transport sector are seeing supply constraints and emerging jobs that our workers can explore in the future?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How are we addressing our human capital constraints going forward, especially in the transport sector?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How does Changi's current air traffic volume compare to pre-COVID numbers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I have read other reports which are less optimistic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: They name several stumbling blocks for Changi, including the strong Singapore dollar that discourages inbound travel, low-cost airline Jetstar Asia's sluggish recovery and regulatory issues hindering the recovery of flight capacity on the Singapore-Jakarta route.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Our head start for being the first in Asia to reopen to international travellers is slowly disappearing, as airports in Incheon, Taipei, Bangkok and Hong Kong are fast catching up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: To safeguard our aviation hub status, we must pay as much attention to quality as we do to quantity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Post-pandemic, many aviation workers are either new to the industry or have returned after a significant break.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As the travel volumes at Changi recover from COVID-19 disruption, may I ask the Ministry how is the aviation workforce coping and what plans do we have to future-proof the aviation workforce?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Singapore has been continuously building on its connectivity as a hub for business and trade.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: With the upcoming Tuas Port and Changi Airport Terminal 5, we are no doubt building capacities for the future by investing in state-of-the-art infrastructure, adopting innovative technologies and enhancing operational efficiency.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: However, to fully realise the potential of our hubs, we must not forget that our workforce need upskilling and clear career progressions so that our hubs continue to be attractive and exciting to new entrants.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Can the Ministry provide us with an update on the Tuas Port and Terminal 5 developments and how can Singapore prepare employees to enter the maritime and aviation sectors while smoothening the process for professionals making mid-career switches?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would MOT provide a progress update on its construction works and whether it is on track to be operational around the middle of 2030s?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would it be possible to expedite the construction process?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Poh Li San, you have two cuts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The purchase of the fuel will be set at a fixed quantum, based on the Sustainable Aviation Fuel target and projected Sustainable Aviation Fuel price at the time of purchase.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How does the longer-term goal and the means for funding the higher cost of Sustainable Aviation Fuel adoption compare with other key aviation hubs?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Is the increase in the supply of Sustainable Aviation Fuel on track to meet the 4% goal in 2030?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How can the cost of Sustainable Aviation Fuels be available to Singapore be kept competitive given the increase in global demand for feedstock and biofuels?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The Academy intends to update its courses on air traffic safety, safety and security and aviation management.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: In view of the high traffic growth trajectory and the opening of Terminal 5 in the middle of 2030s, how does the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) intend to recruit and train aviation professionals to support other roles, such as aeronautical and aerospace engineers for maintenance, repair, overhaul (MRO) functions, air cargo logisticians and ground handling operators?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: These functions are undergoing changes as more advanced technologies and new work processes are being deployed.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How is CAAS working with the Institutes of Higher Learning to ensure that the course curriculum related to aviation are updated with the latest industry standards and practices?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Based on the projected number of graduates from the Institute of Technical Education (ITE), polytechnics and universities, will there be sufficient well-trained professionals for our aviation industry in the next 10 years?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The aviation industry is traditionally heavily male-dominated, with only about 20% representation by women globally, based on a recent Women Aviation International Advisory Board study.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The representation in Asia Pacific and Singapore may be even lower.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: To tap on the other half of the talent pool, are there plans to encourage more women to join the sector and are there targeted initiatives, such as scholarships and internships, to attract and recruit more women to join the industry?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Chairman, I thank Members for their questions and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I also wish to thank Singaporeans for sharing valuable views and feedback during MOT's Forward Singapore (Forward SG) engagements and helping to shape our vision for Singapore's land, air and sea transport together.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOT is focusing on three areas for this year's COS: enhancing our liveability, living environment and livelihoods, by putting people at the heart of what we do.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are also preparing for future challenges, such as climate change and technological developments and to overcome our land, labour and carbon constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Core to this vision is our car-lite strategy, where Walk-Cycle-Ride are the main modes of transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singaporeans also shared their desire for a more inclusive and accessible public transport system, with good first-mile and last-mile infrastructure to support walking and active mobility and to prepare for an ageing society.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our rail network is the backbone of Singapore's public transport system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the past decade, we have grown our rail network by 40%, with the opening of Downtown Line (DTL) and the earlier stages of TEL.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many are looking forward to the fourth stage of TEL.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The seven new TEL stations from Tanjong Rhu to Bayshore will improve connectivity and shorten travel times for residents in the east, such as those staying in Marine Parade and East Coast.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: TEL4 is currently going through rigorous testing to ensure system resilience and reliability before commencing operations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides TEL, the North East Line (NEL) will be extended with the opening of Punggol Coast Station by end of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This station will provide a new link for residents in Punggol North, and enable convenient access to the Punggol Digital District and Singapore Institute of Technology Punggol campus.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We had earlier introduced six new trains, which will reduce wait times for commuters along the entire NEL.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Minister of State Low Yen Ling and her residents will also be happy to know we will open Hume station on the DTL next year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will bring the MRT closer to more residents over the next few years, but our task is not without challenges as many projects were delayed by the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes the TEL Stage 5 and Downtown Line Stage 3 extension which will link these two lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have tried our best to catch up and to overcome the construction challenges of tunnelling in close proximity to existing critical infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will open Bedok South, Sungei Bedok and Xilin Stations in 2026.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: LTA will also close the loop of the Circle Line and open three new stations in 2026 – Keppel, Cantonment and Prince Edward – between the existing HarbourFront and Marina Bay stations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To facilitate integration works, we are temporarily closing one platform each at Telok Blangah and HarbourFront stations from January to May this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When we complete the full circle, commuters can enjoy more direct routes to the city centre.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides connectivity, the rail network must continue to provide reliable service.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last year, we completed major renewal works on the North-South and East-West Lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This project took more than a decade, through close partnership between LTA, SMRT, manufacturers and contractors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Bukit Panjang Light Rail Transit (LRT), or BPLRT, is also undergoing a major renewal programme to be completed by 2026.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Renewal works are progressing well and we will be putting new trains into service.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To facilitate testing of these new trains, we will implement Early Closures on Fridays and weekends from late March to June this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: BPLRT has also been running on a single-loop service during off-peak hours and weekends since 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Starting later this month, we will gradually resume double-loop service during more time periods.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through Government investment and the dedicated efforts of our rail operators and workers, the MRT network has maintained a Mean Kilometres-Between-Failure, or MKBF, of over one million train-kilometres since 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is comparable to some of the world's best metro systems.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: While reliability has improved, operators' maintenance costs have increased.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our next goal is to work closely with operators to achieve high reliability while keeping costs sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes developing our workforce and improving productivity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the Rail Manpower Development Package (RMDP).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through RMDP, rail operators have worked closely with the unions to train around 3,300 workers to pick up technical skills such as data analytics and condition-based monitoring.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another 700 workers will undergo similar training this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I want to assure Brother Melvin Yong and our workers that building a future-ready rail workforce will remain a priority.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how we will keep public transport affordable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Two million commuters, including seniors, students and workfare recipients, enjoy concession fares.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also provide public transport vouchers to help lower-income households.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through these measures, we have kept public transport affordable for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Keeping fares affordable without overburdening taxpayers requires us to optimise our resources.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In some cases, this means redeploying buses and bus captains from trunk routes running parallel to new MRT lines, which have experienced substantial drops in ridership, to new feeder services for residents in new estates.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to balance evolving transport needs across different estates to serve more commuters while being financially prudent and keeping overall costs sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To complement our rail and bus network, we will make it more convenient to walk or cycle to transport nodes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As announced at this year's Budget, the Government will invest $3.5 billion in Age Well SG.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes $1 billion over the next decade to improve first-mile and last-mile connectivity in our neighbourhoods by expanding the Friendly Streets initiative and enhancing commuter infrastructure for residents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will elaborate on this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also want to promote safe usage of footpaths, which will become more important with an ageing population.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We accept the recommendations from AMAP on the use of PMAs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are trade-offs involved and we expect pushback from some PMA users, but we must be clear that between ensuring safety for residents and providing convenience for PMA users, safety must come first.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Straits Times had an article on PMAs over the weekend.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It quoted the views of pedestrians, including seniors and also PMA retailers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many agree that a lower speed limit will make it much safer for the community.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is also the feedback that AMAP received from its focus group discussions and I believe many hon Members in this House would have heard similar views from our residents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Demand for PMAs will increase as our population ages.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is why we must take action now so that we can give users and retailers sufficient time to adjust.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng will elaborate further.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many Members have spoken on this matter – Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Ms Poh Li San, Mr Dennis Tan and Ms Yeo Wan Ling.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am glad that Members from both sides of the House agree with our position that safety must come first and that enforcement is important to complement the engagement and education efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Public paths are used by many pedestrians, including seniors and young children.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Cyclists and PMA users should be considerate, slow down and give way to pedestrians.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is not right to jeopardise public safety for personal convenience.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The large majority of cyclists and PMA users do pay attention to safety and I thank them for doing their part.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For the minority who endanger the safety of other path users, we will take enforcement action against them.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Those who ride recklessly on paths can be fined up to $10,000 and/or imprisoned for up to 12 months.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Your job is not easy, but it is an important mission to protect the safety of all path users.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, please continue to do it well, without fear or favour.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will support you and we will back you up.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These provide the convenience of direct journeys for commuters who do not own cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will provide an update in her speech, including how we are making taxis more viable to improve street-hail services for commuters such as our seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On private vehicles, Mr Saktiandi asked if introducing distance-based charging would allow us to increase total vehicle population by a certain percentage, while still achieving our car-lite vision.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In 2002, the Economic Review Committee recommended, "a gradual lowering of car ownership taxes accompanied by an increase in COE supply and shifting towards a better balance between ownership charges and usage charges".

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With the ERP system in place in 1998, vehicle ownership taxes were reduced during the 2000s.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In 2002 and 2003, the Government released an additional 5,000 Category E (Cat E) COEs on top of the allowable vehicle growth rate, or VGR.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, it is not feasible to only rely on usage-based charges to prevent traffic congestion as these would have to be set at very high rates, which might not be acceptable to many car owners.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Usage-based charges need to work in tandem with ownership controls and other measures like parking charges to achieve a more balanced and sustainable outcome for all stakeholders, while ensuring smooth traffic on our roads.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes location- and time-based charges like our current ERP system, as well as the possibility of having distance-based charging in future, which some commentators have suggested.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I hope Members recognise that the trade-offs are not straightforward and need to be studied carefully before a decision is made.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, some stakeholders such as taxi, PHC and delivery drivers will likely pay higher usage-based charges as they drive longer distances.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will need to examine the impact on these groups, though usage-based charging is in principle a fair approach.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As we expand our transport network, we must continue to reduce the carbon footprint so that our transport system becomes more sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are some no-regrets initiatives that reduce both emissions and costs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, other measures require us to balance our climate goals with cost and competitiveness considerations while we move in tandem with global developments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We launched the Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint at the Changi Aviation Summit last month, an important step in our journey to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Ms Poh Li San noted, our approach differs from the volumetric mandates imposed in Europe, or the incentives-based approach in the United States.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: What we collect with our Sustainable Aviation Fuel levy from 2026 will be used to centrally procure Sustainable Aviation Fuel on behalf of airlines operating at Changi Airport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This provides cost certainty to airlines and passengers when there is volatility in Sustainable Aviation Fuel prices and ensures a level playing field for all airlines operating out of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Importantly, we hope it will encourage fuel producers to invest further in Sustainable Aviation Fuel production facilities in Singapore and the region.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For maritime, we will introduce a new sustainability pillar under the Maritime Cluster Fund to catalyse first-mover adoption of sustainable solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In his Budget speech, Deputy Prime Minister Wong announced two other schemes to support sustainability initiatives in the maritime sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, maritime companies can tap on the Energy Efficiency Grant by end-2024, which will provide two tiers of support for energy-efficient equipment.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Under the base tier, they can receive up to 70% co-funding for pre-approved energy efficient domestic port and harbour craft equipment until March 2026.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Across both tiers, they can receive up to $350,000 per company.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, from April 2024, harbour craft owners and operators may apply for loans through the Enterprise Financing Scheme – Green.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This provides enhanced risk-share of 70% for loans by participating financial institutions for green solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On Ms Poh Li San’s question on green maritime solutions, we are preparing Singapore for a multi-fuel future that will include hydrogen and its carriers like ammonia and methanol.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA successfully conducted the world’s first ship-to-containership methanol bunkering operation last year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are developing a national standard on methanol bunkering to support commercial-scale operations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last December, MPA issued an expression of interest (EOI) for interested parties to submit proposals for the supply of methanol as a marine bunker fuel in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Energy Market Authority (EMA) and MPA have shortlisted six consortiums whose proposals will be further developed to provide low- or zero-carbon ammonia solutions for power generation and bunkering on Jurong Island.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As the world’s leading bunkering port, these are crucial steps to prepare Singapore for the transition to cleaner maritime fuels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The other is electrification of our vehicle fleet.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked about the take-up of cleaner-energy vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Hybrid car sales have increased from 39% in 2022 to 47% in 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, together, nearly two-thirds of cars registered in 2023 were cleaner-energy models.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the first two months of this year, 30% of cars registered were EVs and almost 50% were hybrids.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, altogether, about 80% of new cars are now cleaner-energy vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The efforts to expand our charging network in HDB car parks are key to support a growing EV population.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over one in three HDB car parks are now equipped with EV chargers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By end of 2025, every HDB car park will be equipped with EV chargers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These will support overnight slow charging, which remains the main strategy for our charging network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, as Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Lim Biow Chuan noted, high mileage fleet vehicles, such as taxis, private hire vehicles or light goods vehicles, often need a mid-day top-up.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They require high-powered fast chargers, which are now mostly located at commercial spaces such as shopping malls.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But these are not the usual rest spots for many fleet drivers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government will kickstart the deployment of fast chargers at HDB town centres and JTC’s premises, which are frequented by fleet drivers during their breaks and also close to amenities such as hawker centres and coffee shops.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We recently launched the first fast charging points at Toa Payoh HDB Hub and Oasis Terraces in Punggol in January, and will deploy fast chargers at Boon Lay, Redhill, Kallang Bahru, Tampines, Woodlands and other areas. 54.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our aviation and maritime sectors are important sources of good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are also key enablers for many other sectors in our economy, including manufacturing, finance and tourism.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Asia Pacific is projected to be the fastest growing region for air travel over the next two decades.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Changi is well-placed to ride on this growth.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are on track to break ground on Terminal 5’s construction next year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our seaport also broke several records last year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Annual vessel arrival tonnage crossed three billion Gross Tonnage, and Singapore’s container throughput reached 39 million 20-foot equivalent units.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are currently the second-largest container port in the world and the world’s largest transshipment hub port.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our maritime sector’s growth has remained robust going into 2024.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In January, our Singapore Registry of Ships surpassed 100 million Gross Tonnage for the first time and our container volumes have further increased compared to the strong performance in 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We can look forward to three additional berths commencing operations at Tuas Port by end-2024.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are currently 800 workers at Tuas Port, and as pointed out by several Members, this number will grow as operations ramp up.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Melvin Yong asked about connectivity for our workers to Tuas Port.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to work closely with our tripartite partners and Government agencies to improve the transport options for our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, we have improved road conditions in Tuas, and extended the operating hours of Bus Service 248M.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For the Tuas Road Viaduct, LTA will expedite the construction timeline and we will manage traffic demand during the construction.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Beyond increasing our capacity, we need to preserve our trusted position as global aviation and maritime hubs, as companies respond to shifts in international supply chains and trade networks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Given our trusted reputation and strong connectivity, Singapore is well-placed to capture opportunities arising from these trends.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOT is working with other Government agencies and industry partners to further strengthen Singapore’s position as a node for international trade and as a leading global supply chain hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will be a priority for our Ministry over the next few years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through regular engagements with industry, we have identified collaboration opportunities to optimise inter-modal connectivity through our seaport and airport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Currently, the time taken for an air-sea inter-modal transshipment may exceed five days.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, logistics providers face uncertainty in the arrival and departure times, and to be prudent, they factor in buffer periods between arrival and departure of goods.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, for smaller logistics providers, especially our SMEs, booking of flights and preparation of permits are still largely manual and last-minute changes in vessel or flight schedules, especially in the current environment, will add to the duration.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I have told my colleagues that our stretched target is to enable the goods to depart Singapore on a connecting flight or vessel within 24 hours of its arrival.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are many entities involved because there are many moving parts in these operations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But that is also why we need to bring them all together and work closely.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And that is one of our strengths in Singapore – the ability to work beyond Government; with our industry, with our unions, through the AfA, and to deliver results and get things done.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also continue to engage industry players to identify more collaboration opportunities to review our rules and enhance our processes, which can support new business models and innovations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, we will lower barriers for workers to upskill, reskill and transition to new roles into and within our transport sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We expect demand for aviation professionals to increase steadily given the growth in air traffic and opening of Terminal 5.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To Ms Poh Li San’s question on our recruitment and training plans, we have intensified our talent attraction efforts, showcasing the variety of exciting careers available at the OneAviation Careers Fair and roadshows.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Poh asked about the plans to encourage more women to join the industry.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: CAAS will continue to work with partners such as the Women in Aviation Singapore Chapter to encourage more ladies to join the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Melvin Yong asked how we ensure a strong pipeline of skilled maritime workers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our Career Conversion Programme lowers barriers for employees seeking to move to new or enhanced roles by equipping them with new skills, as their companies undergo business transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The programme was expanded to cover functions in the maritime digitalisation, decarbonisation and cybersecurity spaces.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It has also been enhanced to allow 100% on-the-job training, based on industry partners’ and employees’ feedback.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Beyond recruitment, we are working with our tripartite partners to develop our workers’ capabilities and skillsets to seize new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For maritime, the Tripartite Advisory Panel, convened by the Singapore Maritime Foundation (SMF) and supported by MPA, has completed its year-long review with industry partners and IHLs to prepare Maritime Singapore’s workforce to upskill and transform alongside industry developments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A key success factor will be our strong tripartite process to identify skills relevant for employers and employees and develop courses providing workers with these in-demand skills.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And this is important to achieve a win-win post-training outcome for employers and workers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA and SMF have established a Joint Office for Talent and Skills to drive this effort.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To Mr Neil Parekh’s question, as we press on with maritime decarbonisation and digitalisation, we must equip workers with skills to work efficiently and safely onboard vessels powered by green fuels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA will work closely with our tripartite partners to provide the training infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singapore can also play a part in training the international maritime community in selected key capabilities, to grow the maritime ecosystem of talent, ideas and companies here.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For aviation, we launched the Air Transport Industry Transformation Map 2025 last year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: CAAS, in partnership with Workforce Singapore, has launched a year-long sector-wide manpower study to plan for the future of the aviation workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: CAAS is working with the IHLs to incorporate emerging areas such as automation, artificial intelligence and sustainability into their courses.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
