text: We are expanding the adoption of automation and assistive tools for workers at scale across the airport, making jobs more age-friendly and reducing barriers to entry.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we hope this can help us to attract and retain more workers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, we recognise that business costs have increased due to global inflation and a tightening labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have been reviewing our rules and processes to help businesses reduce avoidable costs and save time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Members may recall I shared some cost-saving measures for businesses during the Ministry of Finance's Committee of Supply last week, and also during the Singapore Maritime New Year event earlier this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I believe it is important for Government agencies to be pro-business and to continually improve our rules and processes, to help our businesses innovate new ideas, and enable them to save time, save money and save effort.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It also provides useful opportunities for the public, private and people sectors to work in partnership and to tackle challenges together, which is what we want to encourage under Forward SG.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will be implemented in the first quarter of 2025 because we need to make system changes and legislative amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will help companies to save cost and save time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There will be even higher savings if the volume of goods transshipped via our land checkpoints increases in future.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Additionally, we are allowing Malaysian trucks and drivers that meet relevant safety, security and operational requirements to directly access our container terminals to handle cross-border containers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: PSA commenced a pilot with one company last year and has now expanded it to all eligible companies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: More than 300 containers have been handled under this arrangement so far and I expect the volume to grow over time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It has helped to reduce manpower and business costs for logistics companies, which they can then pass on as savings for their customers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At our seaport, Singapore rolled out Phase 2 of digitalPort@SG last year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes a Just-In-Time Planning and Coordination Platform, which provides incoming vessels with their estimated time of berthing, allowing them to route their journeys more efficiently and save on fuel costs and time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Marine services providers can optimise their resources to minimise waiting times for customers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Again, we want to do something that will differentiate us from other ports and this is one potential area.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through the use of technology, through the use of data sharing amongst the ecosystem, we are able to do this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: All of these can help our vessels to come to Singapore to “catch up” on delays and if they experience some route disruptions elsewhere, they will turn to Singapore as a trusted, reliable hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Together, I am confident that we can chart a brighter future for Singapore and all Singaporeans for many years to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Chairman, let me share how we will build a more inclusive and friendly transport system, for a more liveable and sustainable city.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At last year’s COS, I announced the Friendly Streets initiative to make walking in our neighbourhoods safer and more comfortable, and roads more pedestrian friendly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked about the progress of this initiative.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We began with five pilots, developing the Friendly Streets features with localised task forces comprising grassroots leaders and agencies to address needs on the ground.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Works have already started at Bukit Batok West, Ang Mo Kio and Tampines, and will start at Toa Payoh and West Coast in the first half of this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Residents will benefit from traffic-calming features, such as road humps, and inclusive features, such as barrier-free crossings and upgraded bus stops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These locations have a higher proportion of seniors or young families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will work closely with the community to implement features to meet residents’ needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, the upcoming Friendly Street in Sembawang will provide young families in the area a safer and more comfortable walk between the MRT station, bus interchange and Bukit Canberra Community Club.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Next, in support of Age Well SG and Healthier SG, we will do even more to support walking as the first and last mile mode of commuting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Poh Li San will be glad to know that we will enhance our commuter infrastructure over the next decade: first, by building more covered linkways; second, by upgrading more bus stops with senior-friendly features; and third, by retrofitting more pedestrian overhead bridges (POBs) with lifts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides helping seniors stay socially connected and active, these will create more comfortable commutes for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Today, we have around 285 kilometers of covered linkways built by LTA connecting major transport nodes to key amenities within a 400-metre radius.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng will be glad to know that we will now expand this parameter, to also build covered linkways to connect MRT stations to more Friendly Streets that are largely within an 800-metre radius, and also to some key amenities nearby.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA will conduct site studies to identify suitable locations for these covered linkways, including evaluating the many requests for covered linkways, such as Mr Faisal Manap's.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will also upgrade more bus stops to better accommodate seniors and those with mobility challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will go further to make even more bus stops senior-friendly, especially those near healthcare institutions or in areas with many seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These bus stops will have more seats with arm and back rests, rain screens and wheelchair-friendly waiting areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Since 2013, we have also retrofitted 87 existing POBs with lifts, where at-grade crossings are unfeasible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To manage the high costs of retrofitting works, we prioritised those near major transport nodes and healthcare institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Going forward, we will expand our coverage to retrofit more POBs at areas with many seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In addition, we will continue with road repurposing to prioritise road space for pedestrians and cyclists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: So far, we have completed four road repurposing projects at Havelock Road, the Civic District, Kampung Admiralty and Tiong Bahru.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Along Zion Road, we will widen footpaths and create a new cycling path by repurposing up to two of six road lanes, to improve the walking and cycling experience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will also expand the bus shelter and provide sheltered connectivity towards Zion Riverside Food Centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Along Sims Place, we will repurpose two of four road lanes to widen the footpath and create a cycling path, and construct a high covered linkway to provide shelter to amenities such as Sims Vista Market and Food Centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Lim Biow Chuan spoke on the importance of road safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Indeed, this is one of the reasons why we introduced Friendly Streets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have also taken active steps to enhance road safety over the years, such as by improving the design of roads and raising road safety awareness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA and the Traffic Police work closely with schools, the community and the Singapore Road Safety Council to engage all road users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA also regularly reviews traffic accident data to identify roads where we may need to put in additional safety measures such as traffic calming measures and pedestrian crossings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Chairman, one of our key focuses this year is to enhance liveability through our transport system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We do this by balancing multiple considerations, such as connectivity, safety, inclusivity, while also promoting gracious behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: LTA will construct cycling paths in 23 towns and estates island-wide this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng will be pleased to know that this will include estates in Jurong West.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: While we are expanding our cycling paths island-wide, it is not possible to build dedicated paths for different users everywhere given our limited land.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: When doing so, the safety of all path users is critical.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Where necessary, we will step up our public education efforts, tighten our regulations and carry out appropriate enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mr Gerald Giam may wish to know that we take a multi-pronged approach to shape desirable behaviours and norms among all path users.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: One is through targeted efforts, such as the Path Safety Programme for schools, and wider public education campaigns, like the Move Happy Graciousness Campaign.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We also work with stakeholders, such as the Singapore Road Safety Council, or SRSC, and the Traffic Police, to educate Singaporeans on path and road safety tips through posters, events and social media.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The Chairman of SRSC, the Chief Executive of LTA and the Traffic Police Commander are also members of AMAP.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: On the ground, our Active Mobility Enforcement Officers and volunteer Active Mobility Community Ambassadors also reach out to path users and the community to promote gracious behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Mr Dennis Tan and other MPs had asked about regulations on the use of PMAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They were put up after careful consideration and in consultation with various stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In arriving at this decision, the Government's key consideration is to ensure that users with genuine needs for PMAs continue to be able to use them while ensuring the safety of all path users.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We had engaged key stakeholders, including the National Delivery Champions Association, food delivery platforms, PMA retailers and social service agencies working with seniors and persons with disabilities, or PwDs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Various members of the public have also written in to share their views and concerns.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We would like to thank all stakeholders for their feedback.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Generally, stakeholders understood the intent of AMAP's recommendations and supported them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Nonetheless, there were some concerns raised and these have been invaluable in our assessment of AMAP's recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They will also help us better implement them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I will address these concerns later in my speech.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This will give affected retailers and users at least one full year from today to make transitory arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In fact, we had first announced that AMAP was reviewing the PMA regulations back in 2022.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: AMAP completed its review and published its recommendations in December 2023.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will announce the specific implementation timelines later, but let me assure Members that ensuring a smooth transition is a key priority.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our footpaths today are mainly used by pedestrians, with the exception of some wheeled devices, such as bicycles and PMAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: And among these, PMAs are the only motorised devices allowed, and they are typically larger and can even be more than five times heavier than bicycles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We allow them to access more locations, such as void decks and lifts, as we know that they are used by those who are less mobile.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In this context, there is a need to ensure that PMAs are used by those who really need them and in a safe and responsible manner.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This is what our regulations aim to achieve.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Some have shared that this may be too slow.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For some perspective, 10 km/h is running speed, whereas our typical walking speed is between four and six km/h.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Six km/h is a brisk walking speed, that is definitely not an average walking speed, as mentioned by Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It is a speed that even some able-bodied people may not be able to sustain for an extended period.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We understand that many existing PMAs have a speed limit of 10 km/h.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: There is no need for existing users to stop using or replace their current devices; they just need to ride no faster than six km/h.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: When they next replace their PMA, the new device should have a speed limit of six km/h.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Meanwhile, there are various ways for users to gauge their speeds and ensure they are within the limits.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They can use free mobile applications or get a speedometer for less than S$10.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: More simply, if you find yourself riding faster than those walking around you, you are likely to be above the limit.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This follows the principle that PMAs are meant to replace walking and that they are welcomed on public transport for longer commutes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, given space constraints on buses and the maximum weight that can be supported by our bus ramps, these PMAs must be within stipulated dimensions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This will allow users to seamlessly transit between public paths and public transport.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We do know that a small proportion of users need larger PMAs due to their physical conditions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Enforcement officers will exercise discretion if they are used on public paths.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, due to physical limitations as mentioned above, these oversized devices will still not be allowed on public transport.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Before I move on to talk about the certification requirement, it is important to make a distinction between the two main types of PMAs, which are mobility scooters and motorised wheelchairs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Generally, we have received feedback about the misuse and abuse of mobility scooters, which are three- or more-wheeled devices steered by a handlebar at the front of the device, whereas a motorised wheelchair look like a wheelchair.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The new regulations will not be onerous for users.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: First, this regulation will only be applied to mobility scooter users, which means those using motorised wheelchairs will not be affected.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Second, we will also recognise existing forms of certification so that users need not obtain a separate one.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For instance, PwDs and seniors with mobility scooters subsidised under the Assistive Technology Fund and Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund, will not be required to obtain additional certification.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Third, we will work with the relevant agencies to identify other forms of certification and keep the process of obtaining them simple.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will provide a transition period to give users ample time to obtain certification.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: There is no need for users to rush to obtain certification.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Enforcement officers will also exercise discretion on the ground.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Ms Poh Li San and Mr Dennis Tan asked whether we can automatically qualify seniors above a certain age to use PMAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We do not intend to do so, as there are many seniors today who have no difficulty walking and we want to encourage them to keep walking to stay active and healthy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This is in line with our Age Well SG initiative, to enhance our commuter infrastructure for walking, as announced by Senior Minister of State Amy Khor earlier.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Chairman, I would like now to continue my speech in Mandarin.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: (In Mandarin):   In recent years, the public has raised many concerns and feedback regarding the misuse of PMAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These PMAs are intended for use by individuals with mobility difficulties, but they have been misused by able-bodied individuals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This not only excludes those who genuinely needs these aids, but their misuse has also led to faster and more reckless driving of these PMAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To ensure the safe and sustainable use of PMAs, the Government will implement three measures.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: First, users must hold a medical certificate to continue using mobility scooters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Users of electric wheelchairs will not be required to have a medical certificate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Users of electricity wheelchairs do not need a medical certificate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We understand that some users, for various reasons, such as medical needs or body size, need larger PMAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Exceptions will be allowed with a medical certificate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I also want to reiterate that for safety reasons, PMAs should only have one seat and are for single-person use only.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These new regulations will come into effect around 2025, after the amendment of the Active Mobility Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The Government will ensure that users and retailers will have sufficient transition time to comply with these new regulations and to ensure that the new regulations do not impose unnecessary burdens on those in need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, from now to implementation next year, we will continue to engage stakeholders and help affected users understand the new rules and to transition smoothly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling would be pleased to know that we will also work with the various platforms and agencies to support the small number who are currently using PMA for livelihood purposes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Individuals who do not have walking difficulties should refrain from purchasing PMAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This term, AMAP will continue its momentum to promote active mobility in a balanced and sustainable manner through two key priorities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: First, AMAP will review the weight criteria for active mobility devices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Over the past few years, we have received suggestions to increase the weight limit for these devices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: A recent study done by a team at the Nanyang Technological University also suggests that some PABs, which are within the current weight limit, may not be as stable, making them potentially less safe.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Particularly, PABs equipped with small wheels or built with small frames tend to be more prone to skidding and could increase the risk of accidents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This will be studied very carefully, considering the various trade-offs that must be made, including the impact on other path and road users.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This could include rides in the community or larger-scale events, such as the upcoming Car-Free Sunday.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Engagement efforts will focus on fostering mutual understanding among various path and road users, for example, through ongoing dialogue with cyclists and motorists to promote a culture of safety on roads.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: AMAP plans to engage the elderly, PwDs, young children and many more in its outreach efforts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: While we review regulations and expand our cycling infrastructure, it is equally important for us to behave graciously, not just on our paths, but on public transport as well.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We can all play a part to make daily commutes a pleasant experience for ourselves and others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These new audio announcements will include messages to encourage commuters to offer their seats to those who need them more and to make space for wheelchair users, serving as timely reminders for us to look out for more vulnerable commuters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I previously announced the introduction of a visual communication tool which uses illustrations of common scenarios, such as “ticketing” and “emergency”, for non-verbal commuters to obtain assistance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This would be deployed at MRT stations and bus interchanges to allow public transport staff to better understand the needs of these commuters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Besides hardware improvements, Mr Eric Chua would be happy to know that we are also pressing on with efforts to promote an inclusive and caring commuting culture, and propel the Caring SG Commuters movement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Over the past year, they partnered with our public transport operators on several initiatives to grow a more caring commuter mindset.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For example, our partners supported SBST’s "Travel with Confidence" programme, which offers a Travel Buddy service.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Volunteer Travel Buddies help commuters with disabilities navigate the public transport system by sharing useful travel information and practical tips.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Go Ahead Singapore has collaborated with Metta School to develop publicity materials, creating awareness of the challenges faced by Metta students during their commute and how others can lend a hand.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Since 2021, Tower Transit has offered a Public Bus Confidence Course to help people with mobility challenges board, travel on and alight buses safely.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Over the years, they have run the course for more commuters with disabilities, to help them gain confidence to use public transport.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Under the programme, volunteers guided MINDS students from their schools back home via public transport.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mr Ong Hua Han asked if information and support would be provided to PwDs and elderly during times of train disruption.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In such an event, station staff are deployed to guide and assist commuters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In addition to public announcements, related information is displayed on Passenger Information Displays and physical signages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Rail operators are also exploring the use of more digital display screens in stations to serve as visual aids for commuters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Beyond these initiatives, individual acts of care can make a big difference.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: When an elderly man in his 60s fell unconscious at Canberra MRT station, Dr Lee Wei Sheng and Mr Kelvin Tan stepped forward to resuscitate the man, taking turns with the station staff to administer cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) until the paramedics arrived.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Such proactive and selfless acts make a profound impact on people’s lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Every commuter can play a part in looking out for others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: You too can make a difference to your fellow commuters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Chairman, ensuring everyone can undertake their daily commute safely and with ease is part of what makes Singapore a liveable city.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This is also in line with the shared desire, among many participants of the Forward SG exercise, for a more inclusive transport system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To make this a reality, it is vital for all of us to join hands, show consideration and concern for fellow travellers to create a journey that is not only efficient but delightful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The first clarification is for the Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: With regard to the PMA announcement, I wish to seek clarification.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can he elaborate a bit more, as he mentioned that there will be help for the transition for some PMA users, existing PMA users and probably those who may need PMAs going forward, until the legislation is passed?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: If the Senior Parliamentary Secretary can share a bit more on what that transition process would be and whether there would be publicity material in the vernacular languages, for example, to some of these PMA users who are using it now and probably will use later on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The second clarification, Mr Chairman, is on the Alliance for Action or AfA, which the Minister mentioned.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I think it is very positive that we are working with partners to collaborate to see improvements in the maritime sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And whether the disruptions in the Red Sea – which was one of the motives why the AfA was probably triggered – have any impact on Singapore's port operations and performance?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Lastly, just a short one, to ask Minister, in terms of human capital, whether we have adequate supply of workers to meet the post-pandemic demands across all sectors for air, land and sea, whether there is any substantial concerns about supply going forward?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The Minister shared a little on that earlier, but whether he can shed further light on it.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: There are, of course, clear violators of PMAs.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: For example, as mentioned, PMAs should have only one seat.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Those multi-seater devices, they are not PMAs, they are technically PMDs.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: They need to get registration, they need to pass a test, they need to go for the online mandatory test, for example.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The key is that there is another year before the new regulations come into force and the public should have enough time to understand.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We take the Member's reminder that we should use vernacular languages to ensure that as many people as possible understand.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And not just people who need them, but also the children or family members who will know how to advise them better.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank Mr Saktiandi for his clarifications.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To his first clarification on the AfA, this is something that we started on earlier, under the Future Economy Council, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat, where he encouraged us to work with industry players, work with unions, to identify areas where we can come together and translate good ideas into implementation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the focus must be on something very actionable.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Instead of doing this by ourselves, we thought we would ask the industry, "What are some of the pain points and what are some of the regulatory hurdles and process improvements that you would like to see that will help you to do your business better?" That was the starting point.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We talked to a few groups of industry leaders, trade associations, our union leaders; and from there, we identified and we prioritised what are some of the ones that we thought we would start with first, and then we formed the joint task force and then we worked on it.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I cannot give Mr Saktiandi a time frame in terms of exactly when we can finish this, but we approach some of these projects with the objective of "ASAP".

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because the sooner we can come together and finish our review and come up with actionable items that we can implement, the better it is for everybody.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we need to split it up into a few stages, we will do so, because there may be some low-hanging fruits that we can do first, to help improve some of the processes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think we will take that approach, a very practical, action-oriented approach.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Indeed, I think the Red Sea disruption is something that has triggered a further review by a lot of companies on their supply chains.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But if I may say so, this process started even before the Red Sea disruptions, because the COVID-19 pandemic was the first major disruptor.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will do the same for the Red Sea disruptions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To the second clarification from Mr Saktiandi, I think this is one of the key constraints that we are grappling with – besides land constraints, carbon constraints, it is labour constraints.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In a tight labour market, we often cannot find enough workers, like public transport.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We work very closely with the operators and with the unions to attract more bus captains, bus technicians.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have different, different ways to try and attract and retain our essential workers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But we will keep trying, because we believe it is important for us to have a Singapore Core in our essential services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The other thing that we will continue to do is job redesign.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We need to look at how we can make the jobs more palatable, more attractive to Singaporeans and especially to our young, to get them to join our industries.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think that is the other very important area.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will make full use of the good measures that Deputy Prime Minister announced during the Budget Statement – SkillsFuture and many other good initiatives – and use our tripartite partnership to work together, make full use of those schemes that have been announced and translate those into good outcomes.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Again, I request for clarifications and responses to be short.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I understand that the minimum footpath widths have been widened recently from 1.5 metres to 1.8 metres.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Can I ask if there are plans to widen all existing footpaths, and if so, what is the timeline for this?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I appreciate the objective of this, but I urge the Ministry to not contribute to the din of loud announcements on MRT trains and platforms.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: When bicycles and PMAs are allowed on footpaths, we have the dimension restrictions.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: That would allow, technically, even on a 1.5-metre-wide footpath, two PMAs to cross, to use it at the same time, side by side.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: At the same time, we also need all users to be gracious and look out for one another – cyclists, riders and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I think it was Mr Giam who talked about having to look out, even pedestrians, to make sure that they do not just keep on looking at their mobile devices while walking.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: This is where everyone can play a part so that our public paths are safe for all users.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: For the buses especially, it is not something that is on the loop, playing every few minutes.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: For those with specific messages to encourage commuters to give way to wheelchair-bound passengers or to give way when there is an elderly boarding the bus.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, I have one clarification for Senior Minister of State Amy Khor.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: However, I am not really sure if these new measures are too little, too late.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I hope not because I hope that the next phase of the P2P industry review will provide more good news.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: One of the biggest advantages of PHCs over taxis is that the PHC drivers can allow his friends, relatives or family members to drive the PHC when he is not driving his PHC for business.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Otherwise, we will continue to see the demise of the taxi industry.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is one of the feedback they have given about the fact that while a taxi's statutory lifespan is eight years, a PHC has no statutory lifespan.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And indeed, when we looked at the data, they are well-maintained, highly roadworthy and this is what we have done.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But having said that, as I have said earlier, this is just the first part of our review of the P2P sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to differences between PHCs and taxis, by nature, the two complement each other and they work on slightly different models and approach.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: That is the reason why we are also looking into how we can maintain a stable and adequate supply of taxis because they provide some services to complement the PHCs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They are quite different because the taxis are really focused on providing services, street-hail, for instance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They do this throughout all times of the day, whereas PHCs, you can see that their operating model, it fluctuates.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More PHCs come out during the peak periods; off-peak, not so many.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are also looking at how we can work towards the two complementing each other.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Chairman, I have two supplementary questions, one for the Minister for Transport.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: As the Minister has shared, it is good to encourage and make available the uses of different sustainable fuel options like methanol in the busy port of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: However, I think we are the top bunkering port in the world and there are many other ships that come here to take on bunkers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: What efforts are being made to encourage ship owners, firstly, within our registry of Singapore and, secondly, ship owners that use our facilities both in and outside port limits, to encourage them to switch to more sustainable options?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The second question is for the Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Can I just echo my colleague, Mr Gerald Giam, on his concern about the width of certain footpaths?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Indeed, not all footpaths are as per the measurement that the Senior Parliamentary Secretary just shared.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Actually, just two days ago, I was at a traffic junction when I saw a PMA stop in the middle of the road and was trying to gesticulate to get the attention of a cyclist who stopped right at the traffic light, trying to cross the other way.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Could I ask that LTA do a more comprehensive review of footpaths and consider, in the longer run perhaps, or in the medium term, how footpaths can be expanded to provide for safe and better usage of all devices as well as pedestrians?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, the question about bunkering, first of all, this is something which the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has already set as a target that they want the international shipping industry to move towards.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there is already that impetus for shipping lines to look at how to reduce their carbon emissions gradually over time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Of course, we are mindful that this process has to be gradual because ships that are already built, they cannot, overnight, be switching to cleaner fuels.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, you have to do this in a gradual way.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When they replace their existing vessels with new builds or when they upgrade their engines, that is when they can put in the option for the ships to take cleaner fuels or to take dual fuels.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we will continue to work closely with IMO and with the industry and our unions to prepare for this process.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are a few pieces here that are important.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First is that we need to make sure that the infrastructure is there.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, both the shore-based infrastructure as well as when they come into our ports, the availability of the service, both shore-to-ship as well as potentially ship-to-ship kind of services, will be available.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second will be to look at safety because, as Mr Neil Parekh mentioned earlier, we need to train our workers to be ready for handling these cleaner fuels.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Traditional bunker fuel, if there is a spill, it goes into the water, you have an oil spill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But if you use ammonia, actually, it goes into the air and instead of having an oil spill, we will have a plume cloud.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And the way we handle these emergency scenarios, our workers need to be ready, our security and emergency services need to be ready.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If I may just comment quickly, Mr Chairman, before I invite the Senior Parliamentary Secretary to reply to Mr Dennis Tan's second question.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will try our best to improve the footpath infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If Members could look at different places around Singapore, one of the things is we have been working closely with PUB to cover up the open drains and then to widen the footpaths, where possible, so that we can then have a pedestrian lane and a cycling lane.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This helps to be able to separate the different devices so that we give pedestrians and also cyclists, PMA users, greater assurance, greater peace of mind when they use the paths.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But having said that, it is not always possible because there are areas where, due to space constraints, site constraints, we may not be able to do that.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the key is where we cannot do that or even where we can do that, people need to use the paths responsibly and safely, and be considerate and gracious.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Just to say that that is why we are promoting the gracious path-sharing culture.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Chairman, I have a question for Minister Chee.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: For example, the airlines, why would they choose to uplift Sustainable Aviation Fuels from Singapore instead of cheaper non-Sustainable Aviation Fuels in other airports?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I think what Ms Poh has raised is, indeed, the difficult trade-offs that we grappled with when we were thinking about how to move forward on this issue of Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To do nothing, I think, is not the right solution because the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) is moving in this direction, setting a target for the international aviation industry to reduce carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Domestically as well, we know we have committed to a target of net-zero by 2050.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is important for Singapore, as an international aviation hub, to be able to offer Sustainable Aviation Fuel for airlines that want to uplift such fuel as part of their service because airlines also want to be able to demonstrate to their customers that they are doing the right and responsible thing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the key here is: how do you do this in a way which can be, on one hand, good for the environment, improve sustainability, but on the other hand, does not jeopardise your economic competitiveness?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First is to take a gradual move rather than to take a big jump and then, to monitor closely what is the adoption regionally, globally, and move in tandem with global development so that there is a, I would not say level playing field, but at least there is a more even playing field compared to if we were to jump too far ahead of our competitors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The second one is how do you increase supply because, today, one of the key constraints is that there is not enough supply of Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: How do you, through a move like this, incentivise the producers to invest in new production facilities in Singapore and in the region?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Just to give Ms Poh some assurance, we have looked at this carefully.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the feedback from airlines and from passengers is that this is something which they think is wearable, is reasonable and they think that this is something which allows them, both the airlines and the passengers, to do their part for the environment.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But you have got to keep it real short.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: A clarification for Senior Minister of State Amy Khor.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
